items.q: Which row of the arteriolar-resistance table is annotated 'Favourable for kidney'?
items.exp: The word 'Favourable for kidney' is written level with the decreased-afferent row, whose arrows show renal blood flow and net ultrafiltration pressure both rising. (Book p739)

items.q: The annotation 'unfavourable' appears twice in the table: beside increased afferent resistance and beside decreased efferent resistance.
opts: True — both of those rows drive net ultrafiltration pressure down
False — only the increased afferent row carries that word
False — increased efferent resistance is also marked unfavourable
True — and both rows raise net ultrafiltration pressure
items.exp: 'unfavourable' is printed against increased afferent (↓ flow, ↓ ultrafiltration pressure) and against decreased efferent (↑ flow, ↓ ultrafiltration pressure); increased efferent is left unlabelled and decreased afferent is the favourable row. (Book p739)

items.q: Match each row of the table with the pair of arrows printed for it — 1) Increased efferent 2) Decreased efferent 3) Increased afferent … A) Renal blood flow ↓, net ultrafiltration pressure ↑ B) Renal blood flow ↑, net ultrafiltration pressure ↓ C) Renal blood flow ↓, net ultrafiltration pressure ↓
items.exp: Increased efferent resistance is the only row where flow falls while net ultrafiltration pressure rises; decreasing it does the reverse; increasing afferent resistance lowers both. (Book p739)

items.q: Fill up: In the 'Control' diagram of the table, the vessel entering the glomerulus on the left is labelled ______.
items.exp: The control drawing is captioned Glomerulus with Afferent written at the left limb and Efferent at the right limb. (Book p739)

items.q: The line 'Efferent arteriole → peritubular capillary → vasa recta → renal medulla' appears under which heading?
items.exp: It is written as 'Note: Normal blood flow', immediately after the efferent-constriction → medullary hypoxia line. (Book p739)

items.q: A cirrhotic patient with ascites is given indomethacin and urine output falls. The NSAID block on this page explains this as:
opts: Prostaglandins blocked → afferent dilatation blocked, leaving efferent constriction, so GFR and RBF fall
Angiotensin II blocked → efferent dilatation, so filtration falls
Medullary blood flow rises, washing out the gradient
Renal interstitial pressure falls, increasing reabsorption
items.exp: Printed chain: Block prostaglandins → block afferent arteriolar dilatation → efferent arteriolar constriction → ↓ GFR & ↓ RBF. (Book p739)

items.q: An ACE inhibitor is called 'beneficial for nephrology patients' on this page despite lowering GFR. The stated reason to continue is that efferent arteriolar dilatation:
opts: Increases blood flow while creatinine rises with the fall in GFR
Raises net ultrafiltration pressure and so improves filtration
Reverses medullary hypoxia by constricting the efferent arteriole
items.exp: The ACE-inhibitor block reads: block angiotensin II → efferent arteriolar dilatation → ↓ GFR (↑S.Cr) but ↑ blood flow. (Book p739)

items.q: Each statement about the mediators listed under glomerular hemodynamics is correct EXCEPT:
opts: Efferent arteriolar dilatation is mediated by prostaglandins
Afferent arteriolar dilatation is mediated by prostaglandins
Efferent arteriolar constriction is mediated by angiotensin II
Afferent arteriolar constriction is listed without any mediator
items.exp: Only two of the four arteriolar events carry a mediator: afferent dilatation (prostaglandins) and efferent constriction (angiotensin II); the two constriction/dilatation counterparts are printed unqualified. (Book p739)
